name: Kato
confidence_why: Goddard's 1912 grammar remarks in passing that stress accent is "nearly absent" in Kato, but Anderson's Cahto Dictionary (2018, 2021), drawing on the Curtis, Harrington, Merriam and Sapir transcriptions that actually mark stress, reports a strong preference for penultimate stress with root stress before enclitics, so fixed penultimate stress is the better-supported reading and the 1912 no-stress remark is a hedged aside from a transcriber who rarely wrote stress at all.

catalog_quote: It is well known that syllables of greater importance of meaning are rendered more emphatic by methods which are characteristic of the languages in which they occur. English, in common with other languages of Germanic origin, has a strong stress accent. ... It seems that in Kato and other Athapascan dialects there are similar grades in the force exerted by the muscles in closing and adjusting the mouth passage. It was formerly held that these were secondary effects of stress accent, although such accent is nearly absent at the present time. It seems more reasonable to look upon these differences of enunciation as coordinate with, if not independent of, stress and pitch. ... new_statements.quote: Stress in Cahto is poorly represented in the data, only consistently marked by Curtis, Harrington, Merriam, and Sapir, and very rarely represented in the largest body of Cahto documentation, Goddard's. There is a strong preference for stressing the next to last syllable ("penultimate") of a word. In the case of verb stems followed by an enclitic, including the often-invisible =i nominalizer/relativizer/"definite", stress often occurs on the root syllable. In compound words stress seems to be assigned separately to the two (or more) parts.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Kato (catalog-all-2026-09-12) has an empty rule and there are no existing statements; this source supplies a placement (penultimate) plus the enclitic and compound provisos, so it fills rather than contradicts the catalog.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls by strong preference on the penultimate syllable of the word. When a verb stem is followed by an enclitic (including the often unwritten nominalizer/relativizer =i), stress often stays on the root syllable instead; compounds get stress assigned separately to each member.
new_statements.exceptions: Verb stem + enclitic (incl. the often-invisible =i nominalizer/relativizer/'definite'): stress often on the root syllable rather than the penult. Compounds: each part stressed separately. The author cautions that stress is poorly represented in the sources (only Curtis, Harrington, Merriam and Sapir marked it consistently; Goddard rarely did), so the statement is a generalization over archival transcriptions.
new_statements.identity_note: Cahto (also spelled Kato), the California Athabaskan language of the Eel River group, northern Mendocino County, California; the dictionary is compiled from archival documentation (Goddard, Harrington, Sapir, Merriam, Curtis and others, 1850s-2000s), not from a specified living dialect.
